assumptions: GNFS asymptotics govern the ratio between the anchor and the target size
no algorithmic improvement between now and the attempt
the anchor's core-years transfer to other hardware unchanged

quantum.scaling: polynomial - O(n^3) gates, O(n) logical qubits

rsa_2048.headline: Classically 6.3e14 core-years (45589x the age of the universe on one core). Quantumly, under 1 week on 1,000,000 noisy qubits (Gidney, arXiv:2505.15917).

ecdsa_p256.classical_method: Pollard's rho on the curve group - no sub-exponential attack known
ecdsa_p256.quantum_scaling: polynomial - Shor's discrete-log variant, O(n^3) gates
ecdsa_p256.note: P-256 is a smaller quantum target than RSA-2048: fewer logical qubits, fewer gates. Compact classical keys buy no quantum margin.

regulatory.note: The migration deadline is a published date, not a forecast of when a quantum computer arrives. It binds regardless of whether the machine is late.

attacks.title: Recover a signing key by factoring, then forge an approval
attacks.question: Can you actually break RSA, or are you just citing a paper?
attacks.capability: The victim's public key. Nothing else - no secret, no side channel.
attacks.goal: Forge an approval that the real verifier accepts
attacks.defence: None available to RSA. Key recovery defeats every padding scheme.
attacks.control_note: the identical pipeline pointed at ML-DSA-65
attacks.headline: Succeeded against the classical algorithm; no traction post-quantum

real.note: The victim's key is a scale model; the attack is not. Key recovery defeats any padding, so the textbook signing in toy_rsa.py is not what lost.

steps.label: Victim publishes a signing key
steps.detail: RSA at a scaled 9-bit modulus (see toy_rsa.py for exactly how this differs from RSA-2048)

steps.label: Attacker's starting knowledge
steps.detail: the public key, and nothing else - no secret, no side channel, no implementation flaw

steps.label: Quantum order-finding
steps.detail: statevector simulation over a 18-qubit control register; the textbook circuit for this modulus needs 27 qubits in total
steps.value: 262,144 amplitudes held, measured k=26479, phase=26479/262144, order r=198 in 1 shot(s)

steps.label: Modulus factored
steps.detail: 1 order-finding round(s), 748 ms on this CPU

steps.label: Private exponent recovered
steps.detail: a single modular inverse once the factors are known - no brute force, and nothing the key owner can do about it

steps.label: Forged approval submitted to the real verifier
steps.detail: the canonical vote payload for decision='approve' by signer 7, signed with the recovered key

steps.label: What this does and does not show
steps.detail: the algorithm ran to completion at a scaled parameter. At 2048 bits the same algorithm needs 4,099 logical qubits and cubic gate count, against 6.3e14 core-years classically
steps.value: 2.3e+11x the work of RSA-250, the largest modulus ever factored

control.note: This is the state of public knowledge, not a proof. No lower bound on quantum lattice algorithms is known, which is exactly why the project also demonstrates agility: the response to a break is to switch algorithms, not to have bet correctly.

steps.label: Victim publishes a signing key
steps.detail: ML-DSA-65, FIPS 204 - the project's default

steps.label: Step 1 of the pipeline: obtain a modulus to factor
steps.detail: an ML-DSA public key is (rho, t1): a 32-byte seed and a vector of packed polynomial coefficients. There is no integer modulus, no group element, and no order to find

steps.label: Why the attack has no formulation rather than merely failing
steps.detail: The ML-DSA secret is a pair of short vectors over a polynomial ring, and recovering it is a Module-LWE problem. There is no group element whose order encodes it, so there is no period for phase estimation to find. Shor's algorithm does not fail against ML-DSA; it has no input to be given.

steps.label: Fallback: blind forgery, the best attack actually available
steps.detail: 2,000 random signatures of the correct length submitted to the real verifier. The signature space is 2^26472, so the expected number of successes is 2000 / 2^26472

steps.label: Best known quantum improvement
steps.detail: Grover-accelerated lattice sieving — sub-quadratic at best, leaving the cost exponential in the lattice dimension. This is the reason NIST's categories are expressed against both classical and quantum attack cost.

attacks.title: Record an encrypted file now, decrypt it after the quantum computer arrives
attacks.question: Why migrate today if no quantum computer exists today?
attacks.capability: A recorded copy of the wrapped key and the ciphertext - a stolen backup.
attacks.goal: Read a file that was encrypted years before the attack
attacks.defence: ML-KEM-768 wrapping: the recording gives the attacker no factoring target.
attacks.control_note: the identical capture wrapped with ML-KEM-768 instead of RSA
attacks.standard: NIST IR 8547 ipd - the migration timeline this threat drives
attacks.headline: Succeeded against the classical algorithm; no traction post-quantum

real.note: This is why confidentiality cannot wait for a quantum computer to appear. A signature forged in 2035 is an attack on 2035; a file recorded in 2026 is an attack on 2026, carried out later.

steps.label: 2026: attacker records the traffic
steps.detail: public key, RSA-wrapped data-encryption key, and the AES-256-GCM blob. The AES layer is at full strength and is never attacked
steps.value: n=403, wrapped DEK 2 B (scaled modulus; RSA-2048 would be 256 B), ciphertext 128 B

steps.label: 2026: attacker tries to read it
steps.detail: AES-256-GCM with an unknown key - nothing to do but store the capture and wait

steps.label: Years later: a quantum computer exists
steps.detail: the recorded capture is still valid. Rotating the key in the meantime would not have helped - the ciphertext was already taken

steps.label: Data-encryption key unwrapped, file decrypted
steps.detail: the AES-256-GCM tag verifies, because this is the genuine key

control.note: The capture stays a capture. Note what is *not* claimed: ML-KEM is not proven unbreakable, only that no published attack applies. The system's answer to that residual risk is agility - the ability to change algorithm without losing the data.

steps.label: 2026: attacker records the traffic
steps.detail: the identical capture - public key, wrapped data-encryption key, AES-256-GCM blob
steps.value: public key 1184 B, wrapped DEK 1088 B

steps.label: Attempt the pipeline that worked against RSA
steps.detail: step 1 needs an integer modulus to factor. An ML-KEM public key is a seed plus packed polynomial coefficients over a module lattice; there is nothing to factor

steps.label: Fallback: guess the 256-bit data-encryption key
steps.detail: the AES-256-GCM authentication tag rejects a wrong key. The search space is 2^256, and Grover's algorithm reduces that to about 2^128 operations - still out of reach, and the reason ML-KEM-768 targets NIST category 3

attacks.title: Alter an approved decision by one bit
attacks.question: What happens if someone edits a signed approval?
attacks.capability: Write access to the signature bytes in transit or at rest.
attacks.goal: Have a modified approval accepted as genuine
attacks.defence: ML-DSA verification over the exact canonical bytes (ADR-0010).
attacks.control_note: the verifier reduced to a signature-length check
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

steps.label: Genuine approval signed
steps.detail: ML-DSA-65 over the canonical vote payload

steps.label: One bit flipped
steps.detail: the least significant bit of byte 0 - the smallest possible change

steps.label: Submitted to the real verifier
Verifier replaced with a length check
steps.detail: accept any 3309-byte blob - the 'signature as opaque token' mistake

attacks.title: Forge under an algorithm you control, then name it in the request
attacks.question: Your system supports several algorithms - can I pick the weak one?
attacks.capability: Full control of the submitted artefact, including its algorithm label.
attacks.goal: Have the system verify a forgery under an attacker-chosen algorithm
attacks.defence: alg_id, backend and public_key are pinned to the signer's Key row (ADR-0001).
attacks.control_note: the verifier resolving alg_id from the attacker's own claim
attacks.standard: the JWT 'alg' confusion class (CVE-2015-9235 and successors)
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

steps.label: Victim's registered key
steps.detail: alg_id and public key are pinned to the signer's Key row at the moment of signing

steps.label: Attacker forges under an algorithm they own
steps.detail: a valid RSA-TOY-9 signature over the identical payload, made with a key they generated themselves

steps.label: Verification resolves the provider from the PINNED alg_id
steps.detail: the attacker's claim is never consulted, so the forgery is checked as ML-DSA against the victim's real public key

steps.label: Verifier resolves alg_id from the submitted artefact
steps.detail: the attacker names the algorithm and supplies the matching public key - the same shape as JWT alg confusion

attacks.title: Reuse one genuine approval somewhere it was never given
attacks.question: Could an approval of one thing be replayed as approval of another?
attacks.capability: A copy of one valid signature - no key, no forgery needed.
attacks.goal: Make a genuine signature authorise a different decision, proposal or signer
attacks.defence: Domain-separated canonical payloads: DS_VOTE binds every deciding field.
attacks.control_note: a payload that signs only the decision word
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

real.note: Every field the decision depends on is inside the signed bytes, behind the DS_VOTE domain tag, so there is no context the signature can be moved to.

steps.label: One genuine approval, signed once
steps.detail: decision=approve on proposal A by signer 7

steps.label: Replay: flip the decision to reject
steps.detail: the same signature bytes, presented against a different canonical payload

steps.label: Replay: move the vote to another proposal
steps.detail: the same signature bytes, presented against a different canonical payload

steps.label: Replay: attribute the vote to another signer
steps.detail: the same signature bytes, presented against a different canonical payload

steps.label: Replay: reuse it to enrol an attacker-controlled device
steps.detail: the same signature bytes, presented against a different canonical payload

steps.label: Weakened payload: the decision word alone
steps.detail: no domain separation, no proposal binding, no signer binding

steps.label: Replay onto any other proposal
steps.detail: the bytes carry nothing that identifies which proposal was approved, so the same signature is a valid approval of every proposal in the system

attacks.title: Guess passwords offline against a stolen database
attacks.question: If the database leaks, how long do the signing keys last?
attacks.capability: The entire database: salts, wrapped private keys, everything but passwords.
attacks.goal: Recover a password and unwrap the signing key it protects
attacks.defence: Argon2id at memory-hard parameters, with a unique salt per user.
attacks.control_note: the password store weakened to a single unsalted SHA-256
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

steps.label: Stolen database
steps.detail: Argon2id at the application's parameters: t=3, m=64 MiB, p=4

steps.label: Dictionary attack, 2-second budget
steps.detail: each guess must pay the full Argon2id cost; there is no shortcut and no precomputation, because the salt is unique per user

steps.label: Extrapolated cost
steps.detail: at the measured rate, an eight-character lowercase-alphanumeric space (36^8) would take 4,502 years of one machine's time

steps.label: Password store weakened to one SHA-256 pass
steps.detail: no salt, no iteration count - a design still found in production systems

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: the same dictionary, the same machine, the same budget

attacks.title: Manufacture an approval by writing straight to the database
attacks.question: What if someone gets into your database?
attacks.capability: Direct SQL write access. No password, no session, no route involved.
attacks.goal: Reach the M-of-N threshold with an approval nobody gave
attacks.defence: tally() counts only signatures that currently verify.
attacks.control_note: a tally that counts the decision column instead of verifying
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

real.note: The attacker can write whatever they like into the signatures table. They cannot make it verify, and only verification counts.

steps.label: Starting state
steps.detail: one genuine rejection; the proposal needs 2 approvals of 3 signers

steps.label: Attacker writes an approval row directly
steps.detail: a real signature blob, copied from the genuine rejection, relabelled as an approval and attributed to a different signer

steps.label: The database now contains the approval
steps.detail: counting rows would report it

steps.label: The tally verifies instead of counting
steps.detail: approval_service.tally re-verifies every signature against the proposal's canonical payload, so a row whose signature does not verify contributes nothing

control.note: Two inserted rows, no valid signatures, and the proposal is approved.

steps.label: Tally weakened to counting the decision column
steps.detail: the shape almost every approval workflow uses: trust the row, the signature is decoration

attacks.title: Join the signer list after the vote opened, then vote
attacks.question: Can the membership be changed to change the outcome?
attacks.goal: Vote on a proposal that opened before the attacker was authorised
attacks.defence: The proposal freezes its authorised-signer set at creation.
attacks.control_note: authorisation checked against live membership rather than the snapshot
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

real.note: Membership may change; who could decide *this* proposal may not. The snapshot is what makes the second sentence true.

steps.label: Proposal opens and freezes its signer list
steps.detail: the set of authorised signers is captured on the proposal row at creation

steps.label: Attacker is added to the vault afterwards
steps.detail: through the real membership service - this part succeeds, and should: vault membership is allowed to change
steps.value: intruder id=9 is now a vault member

steps.label: Attacker votes on the already-open proposal
steps.detail: the vote is checked against the frozen snapshot, not the live membership
steps.value: accepted=False (ApprovalError: You are not an authorised signer for this proposal.)

steps.label: Authorisation weakened to 'is a current vault member'
steps.detail: the natural implementation, and the one that loses: it answers a question about now, when the question is about when the proposal opened

steps.label: Attacker's vote under the weakened check
steps.detail: they joined after the freeze, so only the live check lets them in

attacks.title: Edit the audit trail to hide what happened
attacks.question: The log is in the same database - why would I believe it?
attacks.capability: Direct SQL write access to the ledger table.
attacks.goal: Change a recorded event and leave the log self-consistent
attacks.defence: Hash-chained entries: each commits to its predecessor's digest.
attacks.control_note: an append-only audit table with no hash chaining
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

real.note: Detection, not prevention. A database writer can always change a row; what they cannot do is leave the chain consistent afterwards.

steps.label: Audit trail before the attack
steps.detail: a hash chain: each entry commits to the previous entry's digest, and the head is signed by the SYSTEM anchor key

steps.label: Attacker edits a committed entry
steps.detail: entry seq=36, payload_json replaced by direct database write and confirmed re-read from the database

steps.label: Chain re-verified
steps.detail: the edited entry's digest no longer matches the one its successor commits to, so the walk stops at the tampered row
steps.value: chain_ok=False, first break at seq=36, overall ok=False

steps.label: Integrity check weakened to 'the rows are all there, in order'
steps.detail: what a timestamped audit table actually guarantees: that nothing was deleted, not that nothing was changed

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: the entry now says something it never said, and the log agrees with itself

attacks.title: Alter a stored file without the key
attacks.question: Encryption hides the file - but can someone change it?
attacks.capability: Write access to the encrypted blob at rest.
attacks.goal: Change the contents of an encrypted attachment undetected
attacks.defence: AES-256-GCM: the authentication tag covers the ciphertext.
attacks.headline: Blocked — and the control confirms the named mechanism is what blocked it

real.note: The tag makes the file tamper-evident, not merely unreadable: the difference between 'nobody can read this' and 'nobody can change this without being caught'.

steps.label: File encrypted at rest
steps.detail: AES-256-GCM, the key wrapped under the vault's ML-KEM keypair

steps.label: Attacker flips one bit of the stored ciphertext
steps.detail: no key required; this is a write to the blob on disk

steps.label: Download attempted
steps.detail: GCM recomputes the authentication tag over the ciphertext it was given

steps.label: Authentication removed: AES-256-CTR instead of GCM
steps.detail: confidentiality without integrity - still a common configuration

steps.label: Attacker edits the amount through the ciphertext
steps.detail: CTR is a stream cipher, so a flipped ciphertext bit flips exactly that plaintext bit. The attacker never learns the key and never needs to

steps.label: Decryption succeeds and reports no error
